The Double Diagonal Estimator: Reducing Bias in Two-Sided Marketplace Experiments

Saanvi Chawla email: saanvic@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA and Vasilis Syrgkanis email: vsyrgk@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
© none
Abstract.

Interference between participants in two-sided marketplace experiments can severely bias conventional A/B tests. While two-sided randomization (TSR), which randomizes both supply and demand, enables estimators that mitigate this bias, existing analyses offer limited guidance on which estimator to prefer for the balanced market conditions common in practice, as they largely focus on extreme supply- or demand-constrained regimes. We introduce the Double Diagonal (DD) estimator, a novel method for interference-robust treatment effect estimation. The DD estimator contrasts the outcomes of treated-treated and control-control pairs and uses the off-diagonal interactions (treated-control and control-treated) to correct for interference-induced bias. We provide the first theoretical comparison between the DD and the standard naive TSR (TSRN) estimator under a simplifying mean-field market model, proving two key results: (i) DD’s bias is strictly smaller than the standard estimator’s below a critical threshold of the outside-option parameter; in particular, DD’s bias is smaller whenever the outside option is at most twice as attractive as platform options; and (ii) the two estimators exhibit biases in opposite directions, with DD underestimating and the standard estimator overestimating the true effect, respectively. Extensive numerical experiments in realistic market settings—spanning heterogeneous treatment effects, supply-demand imbalances, and varied market structures—corroborate our theoretical findings. Across a wide range of configurations, the DD estimator demonstrates the lowest bias, establishing it as a robust and often superior choice for reliable experimentation in two-sided marketplaces.

1. Introduction

Two-sided platforms, including lodging marketplaces like Airbnb, freelancing platforms like Upwork, and ride-sharing services like Uber, routinely employ A/B testing to evaluate interventions that affect interactions between buyers and sellers. The fundamental challenge in these experiments is interference: the treatment assigned to one market participant influences outcomes for other participants through competition for scarce resources. When a seller’s listing becomes more attractive due to treatment, it may “steal” bookings from control listings, inflating the apparent treatment effect. This violation of the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) (Imbens and Rubin, 2015) renders naive estimators biased, sometimes by factors of two or more (Blake and Coey, 2014).

Prior work has established that the direction and magnitude of bias depend critically on market balance. Johari et al. (2021) developed a mean field framework showing that customer-side randomization (CR) is unbiased in highly demand-constrained markets while listing-side randomization (LR) is unbiased in highly supply-constrained markets. They introduced Two-Sided Randomization (TSR), which randomizes both customers and listings simultaneously, along with a naive TSR estimator (TSRN). While TSR represents an important advance, the question of optimal estimator design remains open: Can we do better than existing approaches?

Our Contributions.

We introduce the Double Diagonal (DD) estimator and provide rigorous theoretical and empirical evidence that it achieves lower bias than TSRN across a wide range of market conditions:

  1. (1)

    A novel estimator. We propose the Double Diagonal estimator, which contrasts the outcomes of treated-treated and control-control pairs and uses off-diagonal interactions to correct for interference-induced bias.

  2. (2)

    Theoretical bias characterization. We prove that for small treatment effects: (i) DD systematically underestimates the true treatment effect (BiasDD<0\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{DD}}<0), while (ii) TSRN systematically overestimates (BiasTSRN>0\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{TSRN}}>0).

  3. (3)

    Explicit optimality threshold. We prove the existence of a unique critical threshold a∗​(αL)a^{*}(\alpha_{L}) such that |BiasDD|<|BiasTSRN||\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{DD}}|<|\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{TSRN}}| for all a<a∗​(αL)a<a^{*}(\alpha_{L}). At αL=12\alpha_{L}=\frac{1}{2}, we derive a∗≈2.34a^{*}\approx 2.34, meaning DD’s bias is smaller whenever the outside option is at most about twice as attractive as platform options.

  4. (4)

    Experimental validation. Extensive numerical experiments across diverse market configurations corroborate our theoretical findings, with DD achieving the lowest bias in most scenarios.

Organization.

Section 3 presents the mean field market model. Section 4 describes two-sided experimental design. Section 5 defines the estimators. Section 7 contains our main theoretical results. Section 8 presents experimental evaluation. Section 9 concludes.

2. Related Work

Johari et al. (2021) develop an analytical framework for experimental design in two-sided platforms using a mean-field market model. They show that the bias of standard one-sided estimators depends critically on market balance: customer-side randomization (CR) is unbiased in highly demand-constrained markets, while listing-side randomization (LR) is unbiased in highly supply-constrained markets. They introduce two-sided randomization (TSR), where both customers and listings are independently assigned to treatment and control, and propose a naive TSR estimator (TSRN) along with improved interpolating estimators that heuristically correct for interference. Our work builds directly on this framework: we adopt the same mean-field market model and TSR experimental design, but ask a different question—given that two-sided randomization is employed, which estimator should the platform use? We introduce the Double Diagonal (DD) estimator, which aggregates bookings by listing cohort rather than by customer-listing combination, and provide the first theoretical comparison between DD and TSRN. While Johari et al. characterize bias in the limiting regimes of extreme market imbalance, our results address the practically important intermediate regime, proving that DD has strictly lower bias than TSRN below a critical threshold of the outside-option parameter and that the two estimators exhibit biases in opposite directions.

Masoero et al. (2026) provide the first formal finite-sample analysis of Multiple Randomization Designs (MRDs), a general class of experimental designs for marketplaces with multiple interacting populations. Under a local interference assumption, where the outcome of a buyer-seller pair depends only on its own treatment assignment and the fractions of treated buyers and sellers, they derive exact finite-sample variances for plug-in estimators of causal effects in Simple MRDs (SMRDs), propose conservative variance estimators, and prove design-based central limit theorems. Their analysis is design-based and nonparametric, placing no distributional assumptions on potential outcomes, and they show that SMRDs can detect and measure spillover effects that single-sided designs cannot identify. Our work is complementary: while Masoero et al. focus on variance characterization and inference under local interference, we focus on bias characterization under a parametric mean-field model and analyze bias with respect to Global Treatment and Control. The DD estimator we propose can be expressed within the SMRD framework of Masoero et al., where it corresponds to a specific linear combination of the four cohort-level averages, and the finite-sample inference tools they develop could in principle be applied to conduct valid inference for DD. The MRD framework is also discussed in the review by Bajari et al. (2023), who introduce MRDs and discuss their application to marketplace experimentation more broadly.

Several recent papers study interference and bias correction specifically in two-sided marketplace experiments. Li et al. (2022) develop a tractable market model to study how the choice of experiment side (supply vs. demand) and treatment proportion affect both bias and variance, providing practical guidance for platforms. Bright et al. (2025) propose using shadow prices from the platform’s matching linear program to reduce interference bias, proving that their estimator corresponds to the correct first-order Taylor approximation of the value function and is less biased than the standard RCT estimator. Farias et al. (2023) introduces a Differences-in-Qs Monte-Carlo estimator that formalizes interference correction as a policy evaluation problem and achieves bias that is second-order in the treatment effect. Nandy et al. (2021) propose the UniCoRn approach, a producer-side experiment design for two-sided marketplaces that is agnostic to network density and does not require prior knowledge of the underlying network. Goli et al. (2024) propose a bias-correction approach that leverages data across multiple experiments to identify observations near partial equilibrium. Our work differs from these approaches in that we do not change experimental design or introduce a post-hoc bias correction method; instead, we introduce a new estimator for the existing TSR design and provide theoretical guarantees on when it dominates the standard alternative.

Foundational work on interference in randomized experiments includes (Rosenbaum, 2007; Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Manski, 2013; Ugander et al., 2013; Eckles et al., 2017), which developed frameworks for understanding how treatment spillovers violate the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA). More recently, researchers have focused specifically on two-sided marketplace settings, where interference arises from equilibrium effects between supply and demand (Johari et al., 2024; Wager and Xu, 2021; Bajari et al., 2023; Munro et al., 2025; Shirani and Bayati, 2024). Several studies have characterized the bias in estimating global treatment effects (GTE) from platform experiments when treatments are sign-consistent (Hu et al., 2022; Aronow and Samii, 2017; Han et al., 2023; Johari et al., 2017). We contribute to this literature by providing a theoretical comparison between competing TSR estimators under balanced market conditions and deriving conditions under which different estimators are preferred based on the market’s outside-option parameter.

Finally, a related line of work studies interference through the lens of bipartite experimental designs. Doudchenko et al. (2020) and Zigler and Papadogeorgou (2020) develop causal inference methods for bipartite experiments, where treatment is applied to one set of units (e.g., sellers) and outcomes are measured on a different set (e.g., buyers). Doudchenko et al. leverage the generalized propensity score literature to obtain unbiased estimates of causal effects for bipartite experiments and construct confidence sets with proper coverage probabilities. These bipartite designs are particularly natural in marketplace settings where assigning treatment on one side and measuring outcomes on the other can better account for cross-side interference. While this line of work models interference through a fixed bipartite graph structure connecting two populations, our setting captures interference that arises endogenously through dynamic competition for limited inventory, where the interference pattern itself depends on the experimental design and market conditions.

3. The Mean Field Market Model

We adopt the mean field market model introduced by Johari et al. (2021). This section provides a complete description of the model primitives, dynamics, and steady-state characterization.

3.1. Model Primitives

Consider a marketplace with nn customer types and mm listing types operating in continuous time.

Listings.

There is a unit mass of listings distributed across types according to ρ=(ρ1,…,ρm)\rho=(\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{m}) where ∑jρj=1\sum_{j}\rho_{j}=1. The state of the market is the vector s=(s1,…,sm)s=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}) representing the mass of available (unoccupied) listings of each type. From the mass ρj−sj\rho_{j}-s_{j} of occupied listings of type jj, a fraction τj\tau_{j} returns to the market per unit time.

Customers.

A mass μ\mu of customers arrives per unit time, with types distributed according to ϕ=(ϕ1,…,ϕn)\phi=(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}) where ∑iϕi=1\sum_{i}\phi_{i}=1. Each arriving customer of type ii chooses among available listings according to the choice probability:

(1) πi​j​(s)=Pi​j⋅sjϵi+∑kPi​k⋅sk,\pi_{ij}(s)=\frac{P_{ij}\cdot s_{j}}{\epsilon_{i}+\sum_{k}P_{ik}\cdot s_{k}},

where Pi​j≥0P_{ij}\geq 0 is the matching propensity between customer type ii and listing type jj, and ϵi>0\epsilon_{i}>0 is the outside option value for customer type ii (representing the utility of not booking).

Remark 1 (Microfoundation).

The choice probability (1) arises from an attention-logit model: each listing of type jj enters customer ii’s consideration set with probability αi​j\alpha_{ij}, and the customer chooses proportionally to values vi​jv_{ij} among considered listings. With sjs_{j} available listings, the expected consideration set contains αi​j​sj\alpha_{ij}s_{j} listings of type jj, yielding (1) with Pi​j=vi​j​αi​jP_{ij}=v_{ij}\alpha_{ij}.

3.2. Platform Dynamics

The market state evolves according to the balance between listings returning to availability and listings being booked. In the infinitesimal time interval [t,t+η][t,t+\eta]:

(2) st+η=st+η⋅d​std​t,s_{t+\eta}=s_{t}+\eta\cdot\frac{ds_{t}}{dt},

where the rate of change comprises two components:

  1. (1)

    Inflow: Occupied listings of type jj return at rate (ρj−sj)​τj(\rho_{j}-s_{j})\tau_{j}.

  2. (2)

    Outflow: Available listings of type jj are booked at rate μ​∑iϕi​πi​j​(s)\mu\sum_{i}\phi_{i}\pi_{ij}(s).

The dynamics are therefore:

(3) d​sd​t=(ρ−s)⋅τ−μ​∑iϕi⋅πi​(s),\frac{ds}{dt}=(\rho-s)\cdot\tau-\mu\sum_{i}\phi_{i}\cdot\pi_{i}(s),

where πi​(s)=(πi​1​(s),…,πi​m​(s))\pi_{i}(s)=(\pi_{i1}(s),\ldots,\pi_{im}(s)) is the vector of choice probabilities for customer type ii.

3.3. Steady-State Equilibrium

The dynamical system (3) admits a unique steady state s∗s^{*} characterized by zero net flow:

(4) (ρ−s∗)⋅τ=μ​∑iϕi⋅πi​(s∗).(\rho-s^{*})\cdot\tau=\mu\sum_{i}\phi_{i}\cdot\pi_{i}(s^{*}).

The left side represents the rate at which listings become available; the right side represents the rate at which they are booked. Note that for a homogeneous turnover rate τ\tau, the steady state s∗s^{*} only depends on the ratio μ/τ\mu/\tau. Hence, without loss of generality, we can normalize the model such that τ=1\tau=1. For any general (τ,μ)(\tau,\mu) model, we can always analyze the rescaled model (1,μ/τ)(1,\mu/\tau). Such a model will have the same steady state equilibrium s∗s^{*} and the booking rate of every listing type will simply be a scaled version of the booking rate under the original model. Such uniform re-scalings of the booking rates across listing types will not affect any of our downstream analyses. Hence, in the remainder of the paper we make the following simplifying convention:

Assumption 1 (Normalization, without loss of generality).

We assume that τ=1\tau=1.

3.4. Platform Objective and Global Treatment Effect

The platform’s objective is to maximize the steady-state booking rate:

(5) Q=\displaystyle Q=~ ∑j=1mQj,\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}Q_{j}, Qj≔\displaystyle Q_{j}\coloneqq~ μ​∑iϕi⋅πi​j​(s∗).\displaystyle\mu\sum_{i}\phi_{i}\cdot\pi_{ij}(s^{*}).

Any intervention, such as displaying a superhost badge or modifying search rankings, affects the matching propensity matrix PP, which in turn affects the steady state s∗s^{*} and hence the booking rate QQ. Consider an intervention that changes the matching matrix from PP (control) to P~\tilde{P} (treatment).

Definition 0 (Global Treatment Effect).

Let scontrol∗s^{*}_{\text{control}} denote the steady state under PP and streatment∗s^{*}_{\text{treatment}} the steady state under P~\tilde{P}. The Global Treatment Effect (GTE) is:

(6) GTE=Qtreatment−Qcontrol,\text{GTE}=Q_{\text{treatment}}-Q_{\text{control}},

where QtreatmentQ_{\text{treatment}} and QcontrolQ_{\text{control}} are the booking rates at the respective steady states.

The GTE represents the causal effect of deploying the treatment globally to all customers and listings on the platform. It will also be convenient for our analysis to relate it to the steady state availability of listings.

Lemma 0.

Under the mean field market model the GTE is equal to the difference between steady state available inventory under control, vs. steady state available inventory under treatment:

(7) G​T​E=∑j=1mscontrol,j∗−∑j=1mstreatment,j∗\displaystyle GTE=\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{\text{control},j}^{*}-\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{\text{treatment},j}^{*}

i.e., it measures how many less total listings remain available on the platform in steady state.

Proof.

Note that by the Steady-State equilibrium condition (with the normalization τ=1\tau=1), we have that under global treatment and global control correspondingly, for any listing type j∈[m]j\in[m]:

ρj−streatment,j∗=\displaystyle\rho_{j}-s_{\text{treatment},j}^{*}=~ Qtreatment,j\displaystyle Q_{\text{treatment},j} ρj−scontrol,j∗=\displaystyle\rho_{j}-s_{\text{control},j}^{*}=~ Qcontrol,j\displaystyle Q_{\text{control},j}

Subtracting the two equations and summing across j∈[m]j\in[m] yields the result. ∎

4. Two-Sided Randomized Experiments

Rather than deploying treatment globally, platforms conduct experiments to estimate the GTE before committing to a policy change. A Two-Sided Randomized Experiment (TSRE) randomizes both customers and listings:

  • •

    Each customer is assigned to treatment with probability αC\alpha_{C} and control with probability 1−αC1-\alpha_{C}.

  • •

    Each listing is assigned to treatment with probability αL\alpha_{L} and control with probability 1−αL1-\alpha_{L}.

  • •

    The new technology P~\tilde{P} is applied only when a treatment customer considers a treatment listing; all other interactions use the control technology PP.

4.1. Experimental Dynamics

Under the TSRE, we can model the system by simply introducing “doubled” type spaces: customer types (i,d)(i,d) for i∈[n]i\in[n], d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\} and listing types (j,z)(j,z) for j∈[m]j\in[m], z∈{0,1}z\in\{0,1\}, where d,z=1d,z=1 indicates treatment assignment. In this doubled type space, the experimental matching matrix is:

(8) Pe=(PPPP~),P_{e}=\begin{pmatrix}P&P\\ P&\tilde{P}\end{pmatrix},

where rows correspond to customer cohorts (control, treatment) and columns to listing cohorts. The arrival rates and masses of these doubled types become:

(9) ϕi,0\displaystyle\phi_{i,0} =ϕi​(1−αC),\displaystyle=\phi_{i}(1-\alpha_{C}), ϕi,1\displaystyle\phi_{i,1} =ϕi​αC,\displaystyle=\phi_{i}\alpha_{C},
(10) ρj,0\displaystyle\rho_{j,0} =ρj​(1−αL),\displaystyle=\rho_{j}(1-\alpha_{L}), ρj,1\displaystyle\rho_{j,1} =ρj​αL.\displaystyle=\rho_{j}\alpha_{L}.

4.2. Booking Rate Decomposition

Under the experiment, let se∗s^{*}_{e} denote the steady state. The total booking rate decomposes across cohort pairs:

(11) Q=(Q00Q01Q10Q11),Q=\begin{pmatrix}Q_{00}&Q_{01}\\ Q_{10}&Q_{11}\end{pmatrix},

where Qd​zQ_{dz} is the booking rate from customer cohort dd to listing cohort zz:

(12) Qd​z=μ​∑iϕ(i,d)​∑jπ(i,d),(j,z)​(se∗).Q_{dz}=\mu\sum_{i}\phi_{(i,d)}\sum_{j}\pi_{(i,d),(j,z)}(s^{*}_{e}).

5. Treatment Effect Estimators

An estimator of the GTE from a two-sided randomized experiment is any function of the observed steady state booking rates between each listing type (j,z)(j,z) and customer type pair (i,d)(i,d). A natural class of estimators also considered in the seminal works of Johari et al. (2021); Masoero et al. (2026) on two-sided randomization are linear combinations of the four observable cohort-level booking rates Q00Q_{00}, Q01Q_{01}, Q10Q_{10}, and Q11Q_{11}. We will restrict our investigation to such estimators. The central question of our work is: which linear combination has the smallest bias relative to the true GTE under the mean field structural model?

In this section, we review several estimators proposed in prior work and which have only been analyzed theoretically, in terms of bias, in extreme market regimes. In Section 6, we introduce the Double Diagonal (DD) estimator, our proposed answer to this question.

5.1. The Naive TSR (TSRN) Estimator

The Naive Two-Sided Randomization estimator (Johari et al., 2021) treats the (1,1)(1,1) cell as representative of global treatment:

(13) GTE^TSRN=Q11αC⋅αL−Q01+Q10+Q001−αC⋅αL.\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{TSRN}}=\frac{Q_{11}}{\alpha_{C}\cdot\alpha_{L}}-\frac{Q_{01}+Q_{10}+Q_{00}}{1-\alpha_{C}\cdot\alpha_{L}}.

The intuition is that only treated customer–treated listing pairs experience the treatment technology, while all other pairs experience control.

5.2. One-Sided Estimators

One-sided estimators condition on the subset of treated units on one side of the market and look at the difference in booking rates on the other side:

(14) GTE^CR\displaystyle\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{CR}} =Q11αC⋅αL−Q01(1−αC)⋅αL(Customer Randomization),\displaystyle=\frac{Q_{11}}{\alpha_{C}\cdot\alpha_{L}}-\frac{Q_{01}}{(1-\alpha_{C})\cdot\alpha_{L}}\quad\text{(Customer Randomization)},
(15) GTE^LR\displaystyle\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{LR}} =Q11αC⋅αL−Q10αC⋅(1−αL)(Listing Randomization).\displaystyle=\frac{Q_{11}}{\alpha_{C}\cdot\alpha_{L}}-\frac{Q_{10}}{\alpha_{C}\cdot(1-\alpha_{L})}\quad\text{(Listing Randomization)}.

5.3. The TSRI-k Estimators

(Johari et al., 2021) introduce the TSRI-k (Two-Sided Randomization Improved) family of estimators, which incorporate corrections for interference effects by interpolating between customer-side and listing-side perspectives based on market balance. Define the normalized cell booking rates:

(16) Q¯i​j=Qi​jaC[i=1](1−aC)[i=0]⋅aL[j=1](1−aL)[j=0],\bar{Q}_{ij}=\frac{Q_{ij}}{a_{C}^{[i=1]}(1-a_{C})^{[i=0]}\cdot a_{L}^{[j=1]}(1-a_{L})^{[j=0]}},

where [i=1][i=1] denotes the indicator function. The TSRI-k estimator is:

GTE^TSRI-​k\displaystyle\widehat{\text{GTE}}_{\text{TSRI-}k} =β⁡[Q¯11−Q¯01−k⁡(1−β)​(Q¯00−Q¯01)]\displaystyle=\beta\left[\bar{Q}_{11}-\bar{Q}_{01}-k(1-\beta)(\bar{Q}_{00}-\bar{Q}_{01})\right]
(17) +(1−β)​[Q¯11−Q¯10−k​β​(Q¯00−Q¯10)].\displaystyle\quad+(1-\beta)\left[\bar{Q}_{11}-\bar{Q}_{10}-k\beta(\bar{Q}_{00}-\bar{Q}_{10})\right].

The correction terms (Q¯00−Q¯01)(\bar{Q}_{00}-\bar{Q}_{01}) and (Q¯00−Q¯10)(\bar{Q}_{00}-\bar{Q}_{10}) capture interference effects: the former measures how control customers’ booking rates differ between control and treatment listings (listing-side cannibalization), while the latter measures how booking rates on control listings differ between control and treatment customers (customer-side competition). The parameter kk controls the strength of these corrections, with k=1k=1 (TSRI-1) and k=2k=2 (TSRI-2) being the primary variants studied. TSRI-2 achieves lower bias but higher variance than TSRI-1. The interpolation weight β=e−μ/τ\beta=e^{-\mu/\tau} depends on the ratio of customer arrival rate μ\mu to listing turnover rate τ\tau: when μ/τ→0\mu/\tau\to 0 (demand-constrained), β→1\beta\to 1 and the estimator emphasizes the CR component; when μ/τ→∞\mu/\tau\to\infty (supply-constrained), β→0\beta\to 0 and the estimator emphasizes the LR component.

6. The Double Diagonal Estimator

Our quest for a good candidate estimator begins in realizing the asymmetry of interference in this mean field market model: listings are depletable inventory but customers are a flow. When a treatment listing gets booked, it becomes unavailable to all future customers - both treated and control - until it replenishes. This availability reduction affects all subsequent customers. Customer treatment status, by contrast, affects only that individual’s booking decision without depleting any shared resource. Treatment listings with enhanced attractiveness get booked faster, depleting their availability; this availability reduction is the treatment effect operating through the supply side.

Even though treated listings are sometimes showcased without the treatment technology, in balanced market conditions with substantial inter-temporal interference, we expect that the steady state availability of treated listings will resemble their steady state availability under global treatment in a market with a mass αL\alpha_{L} of listings (especially in settings where the effect of the technology is small). Similarly, given that control listings are never displayed with the treatment technology, we expect the steady state availability of control listings to resemble their steady state availability under global control in a market with a mass 1−αL1-\alpha_{L} of listings.

Given this asymmetry, instead of trying to approximate the primary definition of the GTE given in Equation (6), we will instead attempt to approximate the alternative equivalent definition given in Equation (7). The GTE is the difference in available (global) control vs (global) treated listings at steady state. We will consider an estimator which matches this definition and simply drops the global: we will look for an estimator that, even under the experimental dynamics, measures the difference between the available control listings vs. the available treated listings at steady state (each rescaled by their corresponding population size to simulate the global market):

(18) 11−αL​∑j=1ms(j,0)∗−1αL​∑j=1ms(j,1)∗\displaystyle\frac{1}{1-\alpha_{L}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{(j,0)}^{*}-\frac{1}{\alpha_{L}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{(j,1)}^{*}

These steady state occupancies implicitly incorporate interference patterns as discussed above. The next Lemma shows that this quantity can be written as an estimator that corresponds to a particular linear combination of the four observable cohort-level booking rates Q00Q_{00}, Q01Q_{01}, Q10Q_{10}, and Q11Q_{11} that we will refer to as the Double Diagonal estimator.

Lemma 0.

Under the mean field market model the normalized difference in experimental steady state availabilities between control and treated listings can be written as the following estimator:

(19) 11−αL​∑j=1ms(j,0)∗−1αL​∑j=1ms(j,1)∗=Q11+Q01αL−Q10+Q001−αL\displaystyle\frac{1}{1-\alpha_{L}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{(j,0)}^{*}-\frac{1}{\alpha_{L}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}s_{(j,1)}^{*}=\frac{Q_{11}+Q_{01}}{\alpha_{L}}-\frac{Q_{10}+Q_{00}}{1-\alpha_{L}}

We will refer to the right hand side as the Double Diagonal (DD) estimator:

(20) GTE^DD=Q11+Q01αL−Q10+Q001−αL.\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{DD}}=\frac{Q_{11}+Q_{01}}{\alpha_{L}}-\frac{Q_{10}+Q_{00}}{1-\alpha_{L}}.
Proof.

The steady state equilibrium constraints dictate that:

(1−αL)​ρj−s(j,0)∗=\displaystyle(1-\alpha_{L})\rho_{j}-s_{(j,0)}^{*}=~ Q0,(j,0)+Q1,(j,0)\displaystyle Q_{0,(j,0)}+Q_{1,(j,0)} αL​ρj−s(j,1)∗=\displaystyle\alpha_{L}\rho_{j}-s_{(j,1)}^{*}=~ Q0,(j,1)+Q1,(j,1)\displaystyle Q_{0,(j,1)}+Q_{1,(j,1)}

where:

∎

The DD estimator compares total bookings of treatment listings against total bookings of control listings, aggregating by listing cohort rather than by customer-listing combination. From another viewpoint, the DD estimator contrasts the outcomes of treated-treated and control-control pairs (the "diagonal" terms Q11Q_{11} and Q00Q_{00}) while using the off-diagonal interactions (Q01Q_{01} and Q10Q_{10}) to correct for interference-induced bias. From this perspective, the estimator also performs some interference bias correction. This interference bias correction can be made more explicit if we express the DD estimator in terms for the fully normalized booking rates Q¯i​j\bar{Q}_{ij} that we used to define the TSRI-kk estimators considered in the prior work of Johari et al. (2021):

Q11+Q01αL−Q10+Q001−αL=\displaystyle\frac{Q_{11}+Q_{01}}{\alpha_{L}}-\frac{Q_{10}+Q_{00}}{1-\alpha_{L}}=~ αC​Q¯11+(1−αC)​Q¯01−αC​Q¯10−(1−αC)​Q¯00\displaystyle\alpha_{C}\bar{Q}_{11}+(1-\alpha_{C})\bar{Q}_{01}-\alpha_{C}\bar{Q}_{10}-(1-\alpha_{C})\bar{Q}_{00}
=\displaystyle=~ Q¯11−(1−αC)​Q¯11+(1−αC)​Q¯01−αC​(Q¯10−Q¯00)−Q¯00\displaystyle\bar{Q}_{11}-(1-\alpha_{C})\bar{Q}_{11}+(1-\alpha_{C})\bar{Q}_{01}-\alpha_{C}(\bar{Q}_{10}-\bar{Q}_{00})-\bar{Q}_{00}
(21) =\displaystyle=~ Q¯11−Q¯00⏟Diagonal Effect−(1−αC)​(Q¯11−Q¯01)⏟CR effect−αC​(Q¯10−Q¯00)⏟Spillover effect\displaystyle\underbrace{\bar{Q}_{11}-\bar{Q}_{00}}_{\text{Diagonal Effect}}-(1-\alpha_{C})\underbrace{(\bar{Q}_{11}-\bar{Q}_{01})}_{\text{CR effect}}-\alpha_{C}\underbrace{(\bar{Q}_{10}-\bar{Q}_{00})}_{\text{Spillover effect}}

The diagonal estimator calculates the diagonal effect between (treated, treated) and (control, control) pairs, then removes part of that effect that can be attributed to treated listings being exposed without the innovation to control customers. It also removes another part that can be attributed to spillover effects due to control listings competing with treated listings when exposed to treated customers.

These correction terms carry important interference bias information. Given the description of the DD estimator as difference in booking rates between treated listings vs. control listings in a two-sided randomized experiment, one might wonder: would it not then make sense to simply run one-sided listing randomization (i.e. set αC=1\alpha_{C}=1) and measure the effect between treated and control listings? Wouldn’t that also have a similarly small bias as the DD estimator? As we depict in Figure 1, such an approach would have a larger bias in measuring the treatment effect. Intuitively, such an approach does not contain any interference bias signals and uses strictly less information than the DD estimator in a two-sided design.

Why does TSRN’s customer-side normalization introduce bias? TSRN divides Q11Q_{11} by αC⋅αL\alpha_{C}\cdot\alpha_{L}, implicitly treating the treated-treated cell as a scaled-down version of global treatment. But treated customers face a mixed choice set, both enhanced treatment listings and baseline control listings competing for their attention. This competition is absent under global treatment. TSRN’s structure models interference as symmetric across both market sides. By normalizing away αC\alpha_{C}, TSRN incorrectly assumes the customer-side mixing effect scales linearly, when in fact the nonlinear inventory dynamics may have already absorbed the relevant interference through the listing channel.

In the next sections, we formalize and robustify this intuition. In Section 7 we consider a stylized special case of the general model in the small treatment effect regime. We show that provably the DD estimator has smaller bias than the TSRN estimator for most natural market conditions. In Section 8 we perform a broad experimental evaluation of the DD estimator in a variety of market conditions of the general mean field model and showcase that the DD estimator dominates over many other candidate estimators in almost all market settings considered.

7. Theoretical Analysis

We now establish our main theoretical results. To obtain closed-form expressions, we specialize to a tractable case that preserves the essential interference dynamics.

Assumption 2 (Analytical Framework).

We assume:

  1. (i)

    Single customer type and single listing type (n=m=1n=m=1).

  2. (ii)

    Balanced flow: the arrival rate of customers equals the return rate of occupied listings, μ/τ=1\mu/\tau=1.

  3. (iii)

    Normalized control propensity: the matching propensity under control is normalized to 11.

  4. (iv)

    Small treatment effect: the treatment propensity is 1+ε1+\varepsilon for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0.

  5. (v)

    Balanced customer randomization: αC=12\alpha_{C}=\frac{1}{2}.

  6. (vi)

    Non-trivial listing randomization: αL∈(0,1)\alpha_{L}\in(0,1).

The outside option parameter a>0a>0 represents the customer’s normalized outside option. With the normalization of control propensity to 11, the choice probability under control and treatment, correspondingly, is:

(22) πC​(s)=\displaystyle\pi_{C}(s)=~ sa+s\displaystyle\frac{s}{a+s} πT​(s)=\displaystyle\pi_{T}(s)=~ (1+ϵ)​sa+(1+ϵ)​s.\displaystyle\frac{(1+\epsilon)\,s}{a+(1+\epsilon)s}.

We will analyze the bias of the DD and TSRN estimator in the small treatment effect regime, i.e. ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0. Hence, we will begin our analysis by characterizing the true treatment effect for any function of ϵ\epsilon, as well as the derivative of the effect with respect to ϵ\epsilon, at ϵ=0\epsilon=0.

7.1. GTE Behavior in Small Treatment Regime

We first characterize the steady states under global control and treatment (see proofs in Appendix A).

Lemma 0 (Control Steady State).

Under global control, the steady-state inventory s^C\hat{s}_{C} satisfies:

(23) 1−s^C=s^Ca+s^C.1-\hat{s}_{C}=\frac{\hat{s}_{C}}{a+\hat{s}_{C}}.

(24) s^C=−a+a2+4​a2=−a+a​a+42.\hat{s}_{C}=\frac{-a+\sqrt{a^{2}+4a}}{2}=\frac{-a+\sqrt{a}\sqrt{a+4}}{2}.
Lemma 0 (Treatment Steady State).

Under global treatment with propensity (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon), the steady-state inventory s^T\hat{s}_{T} satisfies:

(25) 1−s^T=(1+ε)​s^Ta+(1+ε)​s^T.1-\hat{s}_{T}=\frac{(1+\varepsilon)\hat{s}_{T}}{a+(1+\varepsilon)\hat{s}_{T}}.

The unique positive solution is:

(26) s^T=−a+a2+4​a​(1+ε)2​(1+ε)=−a+a​a+4​(1+ε)2​(1+ε).\hat{s}_{T}=\frac{-a+\sqrt{a^{2}+4a(1+\varepsilon)}}{2(1+\varepsilon)}=\frac{-a+\sqrt{a}\sqrt{a+4(1+\varepsilon)}}{2(1+\varepsilon)}.

The GTE is the difference in booking rates between global treatment and global control:

(27) GTE⁡(ε)≔(1+ε)​s^Ta+(1+ε)​s^T−s^Ca+s^C.\mathrm{GTE}(\varepsilon)\coloneqq\frac{(1+\varepsilon)\hat{s}_{T}}{a+(1+\varepsilon)\hat{s}_{T}}-\frac{\hat{s}_{C}}{a+\hat{s}_{C}}.

At ε=0\varepsilon=0, trivially, we have s^C=s^T\hat{s}_{C}=\hat{s}_{T}, so GTE⁡(0)=0\mathrm{GTE}(0)=0. The GTE represents the change in steady-state booking rate when treatment makes listings more attractive. Next we characterize the derivative of this attractiveness at ϵ=0\epsilon=0.

Lemma 0 (Derivative of GTE).

The derivative of the true treatment effect at ε=0\varepsilon=0 is:

(28) d⁡(GTE)d​ε|ε=0=4​a3/2a+4​(a​a+4+a)2>0for all ​a>0.\frac{\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{GTE})}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}=\frac{4a^{3/2}}{\sqrt{a+4}\left(\sqrt{a}\sqrt{a+4}+a\right)^{2}}>0\quad\text{for all }a>0.

7.3. The Sign of the Bias of DD and TSRN

As we note in Appendix A.4, when ϵ=0\epsilon=0, intuitively, we have that sT∗=αL​s^Cs_{T}^{*}=\alpha_{L}\hat{s}_{C} and sC∗=(1−αL)​s^Cs_{C}^{*}=(1-\alpha_{L})\hat{s}_{C} and both estimators return a correct zero effect, i.e. GTE^DD​(0)=GTE^TSRN​(0)=0=GTE⁡(0)\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{DD}}(0)=\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{TSRN}}(0)=0=\mathrm{GTE}(0). Thus, to understand the behavior of the biases in the small treatment effect regime, we will examine the derivative of the bias at ϵ=0\epsilon=0.

Definition 0 (Bias Derivatives).

Define the first-order bias coefficients:

ℬDD​(a,αL)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}}(a,\alpha_{L}) ≔d⁡(BiasDD)d​ε|ε=0,\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{DD}})}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}, ℬTSRN​(a,αL)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\text{TSRN}}(a,\alpha_{L}) ≔d⁡(BiasTSRN)d​ε|ε=0.\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{TSRN}})}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}.

We first show that the derivative of the bias of the DD estimator is negative at ϵ=0\epsilon=0. Thus for sufficiently small treatment effects, the DD estimator underestimates the effect. The proof proceeds by computing the explicit expression for ℬDD\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}} using implicit differentiation of the steady-state system. A key structural observation is that ℬDD\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}} is independent of αL\alpha_{L}: the αL\alpha_{L}-dependence in both 11−αL​d​sC∗d​ε\frac{1}{1-\alpha_{L}}\frac{\mathrm{d}s_{C}^{*}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon} and 1αL​d​sT∗d​ε\frac{1}{\alpha_{L}}\frac{\mathrm{d}s_{T}^{*}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon} cancels out exactly after substituting the steady-state values from Lemma 1. Under the substitution t=at=\sqrt{a} and u=t2+4u=\sqrt{t^{2}+4}, the expression can be written as a ratio of polynomials in tt and uu with all coefficients of definite sign, enabling a complete sign analysis (see proof in Appendix A.6).

Theorem 7 (DD Underestimates).

For all a>0a>0 and αL∈(0,1)\alpha_{L}\in(0,1):

(35) ℬDD​(a,αL)<0.\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}}(a,\alpha_{L})<0.

Moreover, ℬDD\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}} is independent of αL\alpha_{L}. Consequently, for small enough ε>0\varepsilon>0, the DD estimator underestimates the true treatment effect:

GTE^DD<GTE.\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{DD}}<\mathrm{GTE}.

Using a similar approach, we show that the derivative of the bias of the TSRN estimator is positive at ϵ=0\epsilon=0. Unlike ℬDD\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}}, the TSRN bias derivative does depend on αL\alpha_{L}. Under the substitution t=at=\sqrt{a} and u=t2+4u=\sqrt{t^{2}+4}, both the numerator and denominator of ℬTSRN\mathcal{B}_{\text{TSRN}} are linear in αL\alpha_{L}, which reduces the bivariate sign analysis to a univariate problem (see proof in Appendix A.7).

Theorem 8 (TSRN Overestimates).

For all a>0a>0 and αL∈(0,1)\alpha_{L}\in(0,1):

(36) ℬTSRN​(a,αL)>0.\mathcal{B}_{\text{TSRN}}(a,\alpha_{L})>0.

Consequently, for small ε>0\varepsilon>0, the TSRN estimator overestimates the true treatment effect:

GTE^TSRN>GTE.\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{TSRN}}>\mathrm{GTE}.

7.4. Bias Magnitude Comparison

Our goal is to understand the difference in the magnitude of the two biases for ϵ\epsilon close to zero, i.e.,

|BiasDD​(ε)|−|BiasTSRN​(ε)|\displaystyle|\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{DD}}(\varepsilon)|-|\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{TSRN}}(\varepsilon)|

Now that we know the sign of the bias of each estimator for a sufficiently small ϵ\epsilon, we can reduce the bias comparison by looking at the combined bias function:

(Combined Bias Function) Ψ⁡(a,αL)≔ℬDD​(a,αL)+ℬTSRN​(a,αL)\Psi(a,\alpha_{L})\coloneqq\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}}(a,\alpha_{L})+\mathcal{B}_{\text{TSRN}}(a,\alpha_{L})

Note that by Theorem 7 and Theorem 8:

Ψ⁡(a,αL)>0⇔−ℬDD<ℬTSRN⇔|ℬDD|<|ℬTSRN|\displaystyle\Psi(a,\alpha_{L})>0\Leftrightarrow-\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}}<\mathcal{B}_{\text{TSRN}}\Leftrightarrow|\mathcal{B}_{\text{DD}}|<|\mathcal{B}_{\text{TSRN}}|

Thus the bias of the two estimators is zero at ϵ=0\epsilon=0, but the absolute bias of the TSRN grows faster near zero than the bias of the DD estimator. Thus, for a sufficiently small ϵ\epsilon, we can deduce the desired dominance:

|BiasDD​(ε)|<|BiasTSRN​(ε)|\displaystyle|\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{DD}}(\varepsilon)|<|\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{TSRN}}(\varepsilon)|

Thus, it suffices to understand the behavior of the combined bias function Ψ\Psi. First, we characterize the behavior of Ψ⁡(⋅,αL)\Psi(\cdot,\alpha_{L}) as the outside option ranges from 00 to ∞\infty (proof in Appendix A.8).

Lemma 0 (Boundary Behavior of Ψ\Psi).

For fixed αL∈(0,1)\alpha_{L}\in(0,1):

  1. (i)

    As a→0+a\to 0^{+}: Ψ⁡(a,αL)→αL−1αL−2>0\Psi(a,\alpha_{L})\to\frac{\alpha_{L}-1}{\alpha_{L}-2}>0.

In particular, Ψ\Psi is strictly positive near a=0a=0 and strictly negative for all sufficiently large aa.

Subsequently, we show that for each αL\alpha_{L}, the function Ψ⁡(⋅,αL)\Psi(\cdot,\alpha_{L}) has a unique zero (proof in Appendix A.9). Since Ψ\Psi is positive near a=0a=0 (Lemma 9(i)) and negative for large aa (Lemma 9(ii)), the intermediate value theorem guarantees at least one zero. Uniqueness is established by writing Ψ=Num/Den\Psi=\mathrm{Num}/\mathrm{Den} over the common denominator Den<0\mathrm{Den}<0 of the expressions in Theorems 7 and 8, with Num=L+M​a+4\mathrm{Num}=L+M\sqrt{a+4}. The product of Num\mathrm{Num} with its conjugate L−M​a+4L-M\sqrt{a+4} is a positive multiple of an explicit quadratic in aa. Hence the zeros of Ψ\Psi are among the two roots of that quadratic, and each zero is a simple sign change. An exact evaluation at αL=12\alpha_{L}=\frac{1}{2} identifies which root is genuine there, and a continuity argument in αL\alpha_{L} extends this to all αL∈(0,1)\alpha_{L}\in(0,1) (proof in Appendix A.9).

Theorem 10 (Uniqueness of Critical Threshold).

For each αL∈(0,1)\alpha_{L}\in(0,1), there exists a unique a∗​(αL)>0a^{*}(\alpha_{L})>0 such that Ψ⁡(a∗​(αL),αL)=0\Psi(a^{*}(\alpha_{L}),\alpha_{L})=0. Furthermore:

  1. (i)

    For a<a∗​(αL)a<a^{*}(\alpha_{L}): Ψ>0\Psi>0, hence |BiasDD|<|BiasTSRN||\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{DD}}|<|\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{TSRN}}|.

    For a>a∗​(αL)a>a^{*}(\alpha_{L}): Ψ<0\Psi<0, hence |BiasDD|>|BiasTSRN||\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{DD}}|>|\mathrm{Bias}_{\mathrm{TSRN}}|.

The threshold has the closed-form expression:

(37) a∗​(αL)=4​(2​αL2−8​αL+7)+4​8​αL2−24​αL+172​(αL−2)​(αL−4).a^{*}(\alpha_{L})=\frac{4(2\alpha_{L}^{2}-8\alpha_{L}+7)+4\sqrt{8\alpha_{L}^{2}-24\alpha_{L}+17}}{2(\alpha_{L}-2)(\alpha_{L}-4)}.

a∗=43+8​721≈2.34.a^{*}=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{8\sqrt{7}}{21}\approx 2.34.

Moreover, we can also show that the critical threshold a∗​(αL)a^{*}(\alpha_{L}) is a strictly decreasing function of αL\alpha_{L}. Thus, for the practically relevant regime where the probability of treatment is small, i.e., αL≤1/2\alpha_{L}\leq 1/2, the threshold is at least 2.342.34. Hence, for any αL≤1/2\alpha_{L}\leq 1/2, the DD has smaller bias in the small treatment effect regime than TSRN, as long as the outside option is at most about twice as attractive as the platform option.

Theorem 12 (Monotonicity of Threshold).

The threshold a∗​(αL)a^{*}(\alpha_{L}) is strictly decreasing in αL\alpha_{L}:

(38) d​a∗d​αL<0for all ​αL∈(0,1).\frac{\mathrm{d}a^{*}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha_{L}}<0\quad\text{for all }\alpha_{L}\in(0,1).
Proof.

By the proof of Theorem 10, a∗​(αL)a^{*}(\alpha_{L}) is the larger root of an explicit quadratic Q⁡(⋅,αL)Q(\cdot,\alpha_{L}) (Appendix A.9). Differentiating Q⁡(a∗​(αL),αL)=0Q(a^{*}(\alpha_{L}),\alpha_{L})=0 gives

(39) d​a∗d​αL=−∂Q/∂αL∂Q/∂s|s=a∗​(αL).\frac{\mathrm{d}a^{*}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha_{L}}=-\frac{\partial Q/\partial\alpha_{L}}{\partial Q/\partial s}\bigg|_{s=a^{*}(\alpha_{L})}.

We show in Appendix A.10 that the denominator equals Δ⁡(αL)>0\sqrt{\Delta(\alpha_{L})}>0 and the numerator is positive, which implies d​a∗/d​αL<0\mathrm{d}a^{*}/\mathrm{d}\alpha_{L}<0.

∎

8. Experimental Evaluation

We evaluate the bias properties of DD, TSRN, CR, LR, and the TSRI-k family across 40 market configurations spanning treatment effect structures, supply-demand dynamics, and market heterogeneity. Apart from all these benchmarks introduced in the prior literature, we also compare against a simpler Diagonal estimator as a benchmark:

(40) GTE^Diag=Q11αC​αL−Q00(1−αC)​(1−αL),\widehat{\mathrm{GTE}}_{\text{Diag}}=\frac{Q_{11}}{\alpha_{C}\,\alpha_{L}}-\frac{Q_{00}}{(1-\alpha_{C})(1-\alpha_{L})},

which uses only the on-diagonal cells. This corresponds to a variant of the DD estimator, where the two interference bias correction terms from Equation (21) are not incorporated. Moreover, we note that the Diagonal estimator is a special case of the TSRI-2 estimator with β=1/2\beta=1/2.

8.1. Experimental Setup

Market Model.

We instantiate the mean-field model with nn customer types and mm listing types. Each configuration specifies: (i) matching propensity matrix P∈[0,1]n×mP\in[0,1]^{n\times m}, (ii) treatment matrix P~\tilde{P}, (iii) outside options ϵi\epsilon_{i}, (iv) turnover rates τj\tau_{j}, (v) arrival rate μ\mu, and (vi) type distributions ϕ\phi, ρ\rho. Steady states are computed by simulating dynamics until convergence (gradient norm <10−4<10^{-4}). Unless noted otherwise, all experiments use balanced randomization (αC=αL=0.5\alpha_{C}=\alpha_{L}=0.5). In the appendix, we present the results for αC=αL=0.2\alpha_{C}=\alpha_{L}=0.2, which we see are qualitatively the same.

Metrics.

We report absolute bias

Absolute Bias =|GTE^−GTE|\displaystyle=|\widehat{\text{GTE}}-\text{GTE}| Relative Bias =|GTE^−GTE||GTE|×100%\displaystyle=\frac{|\widehat{\text{GTE}}-\text{GTE}|}{|\text{GTE}|}\times 100\%

Scenario Categories.

The 40 scenarios span six categories: (1) Treatment heterogeneity: uniform, differential, and opposing effects and functional form changes (additive vs multiplicative); (2) Supply-demand regimes: from extreme supply-constrained to demand-constrained; (3) Market structure: sparse, dense, single-type markets, and varying market size and dimensionality; (4) Distributional heterogeneity: skewed and power-law distributions; (5) Structural interventions: interventions that alter the matching graph or competitive relationships, cannibalization and new matches; (6) Edge cases: Parameter asymmetries and outside-option extremes

8.2. Main Results and Discussion

Table 1 summarizes performance. DD achieves the lowest bias in the vast majority of scenarios, with median relative bias of 20.5% versus 117% for TSRN.

Performance by Category.

The 40 scenarios span six categories: (1) Treatment heterogeneity (S1–S5, S14–S15, S17–S18, S21, S23, S31–S33): uniform, differential, and opposing effects and functional form changes (additive vs multiplicative); (2) Supply-demand regimes (S6–S7, S25, S36–S37): from extreme supply-constrained (μ=10\mu=10, τ=0.02\tau=0.02) to demand-constrained (μ=0.01\mu=0.01, τ=5.0\tau=5.0); (3) Market structure (S8–S11, S28, S34–S35): sparse, dense, single-type markets, and varying market size and dimensionality; (4) Distributional heterogeneity (S12–S15, S29–S30): skewed and power-law distributions; (5) Structural interventions (S3, S21, S24, S26–S27, S39–S40): interventions that alter the matching graph or competitive relationships, cannibalization and new matches; (6) Edge cases (S16, S19, S20, S22, S38): Parameter asymmetries and outside-option extremes

Table 2 disaggregates results. DD achieves the lowest median bias in all categories, with particularly strong performance in treatment heterogeneity (14.5%), distributional heterogeneity (17.4%), and market structure (20.8%). TSRN, CR, and LR exceed 100% median bias in most categories.

Figure 2 visualizes bias across all scenarios. DD consistently achieves lower bias than alternatives in most scenarios.

When DD Excels.

DD achieves very low relative bias with uniform treatment effects (S1: 0.1%) and heterogeneous outside options (S20: 0.3%).

When DD Struggles.

With opposing treatment effects (S3), DD exhibits 44.5% bias while TSRN achieves 34.5%. When outside options dominate (S38), DD underestimates by 42.3% versus TSRN’s 22% overestimation.

Varying Supply-Demand Balance.

Figure 3 traces bias as turnover rate τ\tau varies from supply-constrained to demand-constrained conditions. DD consistently achieves lower bias than TSRN across all τ\tau and all tested allocation fractions. The DD-TSRN gap is largest when τ\tau is small.

Varying Randomization Proportions.

Figure 4 shows bias versus αC\alpha_{C}. DD achieves minimum bias near αL=αC=0.5\alpha_{L}=\alpha_{C}=0.5, increasing under imbalance. The one-sided estimators exhibit asymmetries: LR struggles at low αC\alpha_{C}; CR struggles at high αC\alpha_{C}. TSRN maintains flat bias but exceeds DD in most conditions.

Four-Estimator Comparison.

Figure 5 compares all estimators across the turnover range. The ordering DD << TSRN << CR ≈\approx LR holds consistently. Two main findings emerge from our experiments:

(i) DD achieves lowest bias across most regimes. DD achieves lower bias in the vast majority of configurations. Parameter sweeps confirm this is not scenario-specific: DD dominates for every supply level and allocation fraction tested.

(ii) Opposite bias directions. TSRN, CR, and LR consistently overestimate when treatment effects are positive, while DD underestimates. This confirms our theoretical finding that the two estimators exhibit biases in opposite directions.

8.3. Limitations

Our theoretical results apply to a simplified homogeneous market model with specific parameter restrictions. While our numerical experiments suggest the qualitative findings extend broadly, formal theoretical analysis of heterogeneous markets remains an open direction. Moreover, we have only focused on bias and ignored any variance consideration. Hence, our analysis is most useful in large sample regimes (relevant for online platforms) where variance is of lower order importance. However, a complete comparison in the small sample regime also needs to account for variance, in order to capture all potentially leading terms of the mean squared error. Systematic variance analysis is beyond our current scope. Finally, our model assumes that the intervention affects only matching propensities, not arrival rates or occupancy times. Extensions to these intervention types represent important future work.

9. Conclusion

We have introduced the Double Diagonal (DD) estimator for treatment effect estimation in two-sided marketplace experiments and provided the first theoretical comparison between DD and the standard naive TSR (TSRN) estimator under a mean-field market model.

Our stylized theoretical analysis establishes two key results: (i) DD’s bias is strictly smaller than TSRN’s below a critical threshold of the outside-option parameter in the small treatment effect regime; in particular, DD’s bias is smaller whenever the outside option is at most about twice as attractive as platform options; and (ii) the two estimators exhibit biases in opposite directions, with DD underestimating and TSRN overestimating the true effect.

Our empirical evaluation across 40 diverse market configurations corroborates these theoretical findings. Across a wide range of configurations, the DD estimator demonstrates the lowest bias, establishing it as a robust and often superior choice for reliable experimentation in two-sided marketplaces.
